claims.event: Native of Xiangyang and pupil of Qiao Zhou who held Yong’an after Shu fell, rejected Wu’s feigned rescue, submitted to Jin, and withstood Bu Xie and Lu Kang until Hu Lie relieved him.
Father of Luo Xian who served Shu as Administrator of Guanghan.
Teacher of Luo Xian, whose students nicknamed Xian Zigong.
Eunuch dominating the Shu court who resented Luo Xian and had him relegated to Badong.
Grand General commanding Badong with Luo Xian as deputy, recalled west when Wei invaded.
His surrender led Luo Xian to mourn three days at the metropolitan pavilion.
His death, with Deng Ai’s, left the Shu cities leaderless before Wu’s attack on Luo Xian.
His death, with Zhong Hui’s, left the Shu cities leaderless before Wu’s attack on Luo Xian.
Wu commander sent west and routed by Luo Xian, then reinforced by Lu Kang.
Wu ruler who, enraged at Bu Xie’s defeat, sent Lu Kang against Luo Xian.
Sent to reinforce Bu Xie against Luo Xian; withdrew when Hu Lie arrived.
Jing Province inspector whose relief force made Lu Kang withdraw from Luo Xian’s city.
Shu worthy nominated by Luo Xian at the Hualin Garden banquet and summoned by Emperor Wu.
Shu worthy nominated by Luo Xian at the Hualin Garden banquet and summoned by Emperor Wu.
Summoned to office the Shu worthies Luo Xian nominated.
Son of Luo Xian who inherited command of his father’s household troops.
Nephew raised by Luo Xian, greedy governor of Yi mocked in Shu rhymes, who beat Li Te by Ren Rui’s feigned defection but lost Shu to Li Xiong.
Father of Luo Shang, Administrator of Zangke.
Jing Province inspector who appointed Luo Shang and Liu Qiao as military advisers.
Appointed military adviser together with Luo Shang by Wang Rong.
Rebel in Shu whom Luo Shang predicted would fail, later killed by Li Te.
Rose in Shu, killed Zhao Xin, drove Luo Shang to Jiangyang, then was beheaded after Ren Rui’s ruse.
Jing Province inspector who brought Sun Fu to aid Luo Shang and camped at Jiangzhou.
Administrator of Jianping who reinforced Luo Shang under Zong Dai.
Clerk who feigned defection for Luo Shang and coordinated the attack that killed Li Te.
Son of Li Te who proclaimed himself ruler at Pi and took Shu after Luo Shang died.

claims.event: Wu general from Xi’e sent by Sun Hao against Guo Ma, who mourned Wu’s fall at Baqiu, submitted to Jin, and governed Guangzhou for years; his sons won him the epithet Zhong instead of Sheng.
Wu ruler who sent Teng Xiu to suppress Guo Ma and capitulated before Xiu arrived.
Preceded Teng Xiu as Inspector of Guang Province.
Guangzhou troop commander whose mutiny Teng Xiu was sent to suppress.
Son of Teng Xiu who petitioned to replace his father’s epithet Sheng.
Son of Teng Bing who fought Su Jun and governed Guangzhou with authority, epithet Dai.
Teng Han served as chief clerk on his light-chariot staff.
Rebel in the campaign against whom Teng Han won merit.
Captured and killed Teng Xiu’s great-grandson Tianzhi at Liyang.
Native of Pinglu who buried the executed Linghu Yu at his own cost, was nominated by Yan Province as a general, and volunteered to reopen Liangzhou.
Wei inspector of Yan Province executed for conspiracy, buried and mourned by Ma Long.
Liang Province inspector who alienated the Qiang as Ma Long warned and was overrun.

claims.event: Raised 3,500 tested volunteers, rejected Wei-era rotten weapons, used carts on the Eight Arrays plan and magnets against armored tribesmen, killed Shujineng to pacify Liangzhou, and later rebuilt Xiping.
Tribal leader whose forces harried Ma Long and who was killed by him, ending the Liangzhou trouble.
Guards general who argued that Ma Long’s troops should receive further rewards despite earlier titles.
Southern tribal raider routed by Ma Long’s soldiers disguised as farmers.
Lüeyang administrator linked by marriage to Yang Jun who slandered Ma Long as senile, replaced him, and was removed.
Marriage connection of Yan Shu when Shu schemed to replace Ma Long.
Heir of Ma Long who commanded the mid-channel fort at the Yellow River bridge for Sima Ying and fell fighting Wang Hu.
Prince of Chengdu who attacked the Prince of Changsha with Ma Xian as a general.
Prince of Changsha attacked by Sima Ying, whose general Wang Hu defeated Ma Xian.
General of the Prince of Changsha who broke Ma Xian at the Yellow River bridge.
Son of Hu Zun from Linjing who followed the Liaodong expedition, helped crush Liu Meng, lamented his daughter’s entry into the harem, and warned Yang Jun of ruin.
Wei general of chariots and cavalry, father of Hu Fen.
Xiongnu central chief whose rebellion Hu Fen helped crush, killed by his own officer Li Ke.
Swift-cavalry commander sent against Liu Meng with Hu Fen as rear support.
Officer of Liu Meng who killed him and surrendered.
Neglected government and took noble daughters, including Hu Fen’s, into the harem; appointed Lu Xing over Jiaozhi.
Arrogant father of the empress whom Hu Fen warned that imperial marriages end in clan ruin.
Elder brother of Hu Fen, noted among six brothers.
Son of Hu Guang famed for enterprise and generosity.
Younger brother of Hu Fen who fought Shu, was confined by Zhong Hui, and died besieged at Wanhudui.
Mutinied and confined Hu Lie and other generals, then was slain by Hu Lie’s son Shiyuan.
Wu officer from Moling who lost at Fenshui, recovered by raiding Dong Yuan, bribed Liang Qi, sowed distrust of Xie Xi, and took Jiaozhi.
Father of Tao Huang and Wu inspector of Jiao Province.
Wu ruler under whom Sun Xu misgoverned Jiaozhi.
Greedy Jiaozhi administrator killed by Lü Xing.
Commandery clerk who killed Sun Xu and Deng Gou and submitted Jiaozhi to Jin, then was killed by Li Tong.
Merit officer who killed Lü Xing.
Man of Jianning made Jiaozhi administrator after Lü Xing, who soon died.
Man of Baxi who succeeded Cuan Gu at Jiaozhi and died of illness.
Army supervisor of Nanzhong who sent Yang Ji to replace Ma Rong.
Man of Qianwei who led the Shu force into Jiaozhi, killed Xiu Ze and Liu Jun, and beat Tao Huang at Fenshui.
General in Yang Ji’s force that struck into Jiaozhi and routed Wu at Gucheng.
Jiuzhen administrator whose stores Tao Huang raided and who was defeated by Huang’s rear halberdiers.
Gate officer in Yang Ji’s force that struck from Shu into Jiaozhi and routed Wu at Gucheng.
Gate officer in Yang Ji’s force that struck from Shu into Jiaozhi and routed Wu at Gucheng.
Gate officer in Yang Ji’s force that struck from Shu into Jiaozhi and routed Wu at Gucheng.
Gate officer in Yang Ji’s force that struck from Shu into Jiaozhi and routed Wu at Gucheng.
Gate officer in Yang Ji’s force that struck from Shu into Jiaozhi and routed Wu at Gucheng.
Wu grand commander killed by Yang Ji’s force at Gucheng.
Sent by Wu as army supervisor against Yang Ji.
Wu grand commander who rebuked Tao Huang after Fenshui and later took Jiaozhi with him.
Fuyan warlord bribed with silk who brought ten thousand men to aid Tao Huang.
Champion of Dong Yuan executed on suspicion after Tao Huang paraded his brother.
Younger brother of Xie Xi coaxed by Tao Huang into writing to Xi and paraded in Huang’s carriage.

claims.event: Advised Teng Xiu’s salt-and-iron embargo, honored Huo Yi’s hundred-day oath for Yang Ji’s garrison, took Li Zuo’s city, opened three commanderies, submitted to Jin on Sun Hao’s letter, opposed cutting Jiao garrisons, and eased the Hepu pearl levy.
Unable to subdue the southern rebels until he followed Tao Huang’s embargo advice.
Swore to Yang Ji and Mao Jiong that he would bear the blame if relief failed after a hundred days; died before he could help.
Surrendered to Tao Huang after the hundred-day term, died of illness at Hepu, and was posthumously named Jiao inspector.
Killer of Xiu Ze who plotted against Tao Huang, cursed Sun Hao, and was disemboweled by Xiu Yun.
Killed by Mao Jiong; father of Xiu Yun who avenged him.
Son of Xiu Ze who marched with Tao Huang and disemboweled Mao Jiong; later named to replace Huang.
Wu ruler who spared then kept Meng Gan and others in his workshops, appointed Tao Huang governor of Jiao, and after surrender ordered him to submit.
Captive who escaped to Luoyang, offered a plan to conquer Wu, and was named prefect of Rinan.
Captive kept in Wu’s workshops and executed by Sun Hao; his son was made a marquis.
Captive kept in Wu’s workshops and executed by Sun Hao; his son was made a marquis.
Jiuzhen merit officer who held the commandery for Jin against Tao Huang and refused his uncle’s call to yield.
Maternal uncle of Li Zuo serving in Tao Huang’s army who urged him to surrender.
Son of Tao Huang who carried Sun Hao’s letter ordering Huang to submit.
Tribal leader near Linyi who called himself king and raided the people, cited by Tao Huang.
Supernumerary attendant who succeeded Tao Huang in Jiao.
Supernumerary attendant who succeeded Wu Yan in Jiao.
Son of Gu Mi pressed by locals to govern the province, who soon died.
Seized the province, killed Hu Zhao, was captured by Liang Shuo and poisoned by his mother.
Chief clerk murdered by Gu Shou after Gu Shou seized control of Jiao Province.
Commander who escaped Gu Shou, captured him, and invited Tao Wei to govern.
Son of Tao Huang, Cangwu administrator invited by Liang Shuo to act as inspector, who won the people before dying in three years.
Younger brother of Tao Wei who later governed Jiao Province.
Son of Tao Wei who later governed Jiao, the fourth generation from Tao Ji.
Founder of four generations that gave Jiao five inspectors.
Younger brother of Tao Huang and Wu commander.
Younger brother of Tao Jun who served the heir apparent; father of Tao Hui.
Son of Tao Jun, celebrated, who rose to prefect of Linhai.
Younger brother of Tao Yan who governed Xuancheng and served Wang Dao.
Statesman under whom Tao You, Tao Huang’s nephew, served as chief clerk of the Right Army.
Son of Tao Yan, magistrate of Wuhu killed by Han Huang.
Killed Tao Fu, the magistrate of Wuhu, who was then posthumously named administrator of Lujiang.
Son of Tao Kang and grandson in the Tao line of Jiao, noted as having his own separate biography.

Commander of All Military Affairs of Jiaozhou
Grand General Who Guards the South
Cadet Mentor of the Heir Apparent

claims.event: Wu Yan, courtesy Shize, of humble birth, faced down Lu Kang’s staged assassin, chained the Yangtze against Wang Jun, held out until Wu fell, then served Jin in Jincheng, Dunhuang, Yanmen, Shunyang and as inspector of Jiao for over twenty years.
Physiognomist who told Wu Yan he would one day attain the rank of Xue Xu’s expedition.
Wu grand marshal who tested Wu Yan’s courage with a staged assassin before promoting him; compared with Lu Xi by Wu Yan.
Built warships in Shu to attack Wu, prompting Wu Yan’s iron chains across the river.
Wu ruler who refused Wu Yan reinforcements; Xue Ying blamed his favoritism of petty men for Wu’s fall.
Jin ruler who named Wu Yan prefect of Jincheng and questioned him and Xue Ying on Wu’s fall and on Lu Xi versus Lu Kang.
Answered Emperor Wu that Sun Hao lost Wu by favoring petty men and reckless punishment.
At court mocked Wu Yan as an obscure Wu general and was rebuked by him.
Compared by Wu Yan with Lu Kang as superior in virtue but inferior in achievement.
Was about to accept Wu Yan’s gifts until Lu Yun objected, then slandered Wu Yan until Yin Yu rebuked him.
Brother of Lu Ji who refused Wu Yan’s gifts, citing Yan’s poor reply to an edict.
Changsha filial candidate who warned Lu Ji and his brother that slandering the low-born Wu Yan would isolate them.
Inspector of Jiao whose death led to Wu Yan’s appointment and a Jiuzhen mutiny.
Jiuzhen rebel leader who besieged the commandery seat until Wu Yan suppressed him.
Zhang Guang, courtesy Jingwu, held Malan Mountain for over a hundred days, became Xinping prefect, backed Liu Shen against Sima Yong, and impressed Sima Yong when captured.
Prince of Zhao commanding Guanzhong when the Di and Qiang revolted.
Administrator killed in battle during the Di and Qiang revolt.
Prince of Liang who sent Suo Jing to relieve Zhang Guang and recommended him for reward.
Major sent by Sima Xiong to bring Zhang Guang’s besieged force back to Chang’an.
Earlier exemplar of loyalty under siege to whom Sima Xiong compared Zhang Guang.
Yong inspector who secretly moved against Sima Yong with Zhang Guang’s help but ignored his plans.
Prince of Hejian who captured Zhang Guang, admired his reply, and recommended him as major of the right guard.

claims.event: Fought Chen Min by ambush at Changqi, became Liangzhou inspector, executed Zhang Yan for losing Hanzhong, was misled by Jin Miao over Li Yun, betrayed by Yang Nandi, and died defending Hanzhong at fifty-five.
Rebel whose revolt led to Zhang Guang’s campaign; his army was shattered at Changqi.
Inspector who esteemed Zhang Guang as the talent of southern Chu and memorialized his merit.
Jiangxia administrator who faced Chen Min’s general Qian Duan at Changqi.
Chen Min’s senior general who opposed Tao Kan at Changqi.
Xiangyang administrator who led the infantry against Chen Min’s army at Changqi.
Wuling administrator who hid warships on the Mian River in the Changqi battle.
Led starving Qinzhou refugees to Chenggu, bribed Zhang Yan, allied with Li Xiong, and pressed on Hanzhong.
Liangzhou inspector who sent Zhang Yan against Deng Ding and later abandoned his post.
Baxi administrator who took Deng Ding’s bribe, lost Hanzhong, and was executed by Zhang Guang.
Ruler who sent troops to rescue Deng Ding and drive back Zhang Yan.
Hanzhong administrator who fled to Weixing and blamed Zhang Yan’s bribe-taking for the loss of Hanzhong.
Rebel whose remaining followers Li Yun and Yang Wu entered Hanzhong.
Follower of Wang Ru who bribed Jin Miao, settled at Chenggu, and with Yang Nandi crushed Jin Miao.
Follower of Wang Ru who bribed Yang Nandi to turn on Zhang Guang.
Zhang Guang’s adjutant who took Li Yun’s bribe, then urged attacking him, and was defeated.
Di king who sent his son Yang Nandi to aid Zhang Guang.
Son of Yang Maosou who, refused payment by Zhang Guang, secretly joined Li Yun against Jin Miao.
Son of Zhang Guang sent to reinforce Jin Miao, killed by a stray arrow.
Son of Zhang Guang who served young as aide to the Grand Marshal.
Son of Zhang Guang with his tactical talent who acted as head of the province and died fighting the rebels.
Attendant official who escorted Zhang Guang’s family and survivors back to Weixing.
Protector who escorted Zhang Guang’s family and survivors back to Weixing.
Yiyang administrator who became Liangzhou inspector, after which Zhang Guang’s kin returned home.
Nanping administrator who petitioned Wang Dun for posthumous honors for Zhang Guang.
Commander who refused Ying Zhan’s petition for posthumous honors for Zhang Guang.

Zhao You, courtesy Yuansun, of Huainan, urged Xi Long to join the campaign against Sima Lun, then under Wang Dun defeated Hua Yi and Du Tao and died fighting Du Zeng and Fifth Yi; posthumously honored with epithet Jing.
Inspector who hesitated to answer Sima Jiong’s call against Sima Lun, rejected Zhao You’s advice, and was killed by his own men.
Prince of Qi whose circular called Xi Long to raise troops against Sima Lun.
Prince of Zhao whose usurpation Sima Jiong called the provinces to oppose.
Headquarters officer who with Zhao You warned Xi Long that neutrality would lose the province.
Registrar who with Zhao You warned Xi Long that neutrality would lose the province.
General of the Left who made Zhao You adjutant, sent him against Du Zeng, and mourned his death.
Fought beside Zhao You against Hua Yi and later destroyed Du Tao with him.
Fought Hua Yi with Zhao You and later sent against Du Zeng, planning to use Zhao Yin as bait.
Defeated by Zhao You, Gan Zhuo and Zhou Fang.
Rebel attacked by Zhao You in western Xiang and destroyed by him and Gan Zhuo early in Taixing.
Preceded Zhao You as administrator of Wuchang.
Raised Fifth Yi in rebellion in Jingzhou, killing Zhao You and Zhu Gui, and was later attacked by Zhou Fang.
Commissioned by Emperor Min and backed by Du Zeng in Jingzhou, he drew the region’s allegiance against Zhao You.
Xiangyang administrator who opposed Du Zeng with Zhao You and died fighting.
Jin ruler who had commissioned Fifth Yi.
Son of Zhao You who died with him and was posthumously named prefect of Xinchang.
Zhao Yin, courtesy Boshu, younger brother of Zhao Gong, fought Du Zeng under Zhou Fang, killed the rebel Prince of Nandun, and was relied on by Wang Dao and Yu Liang.
Recruited Zhao Yin as attendant gentleman and relied on him with Yu Liang.
Relied on Zhao Yin together with Wang Dao after Zhao Yin killed the Prince of Nandun.
Praised by the historians with Teng Xiu for loyalty at Badong and mourning his fallen court.
Praised by the historians with Luo Xian for loyalty and for kind rule at Stone Gate.
Praised by the historians for crushing foes west of the river and foreseeing Yang Xin’s defeat.
Praised by the historians for martial skill and for mocking Yang Jun’s folly.
Cited in the appraisal as the commander whose defeat Ma Long foresaw.
Cited in the appraisal as the minister whose swift disaster Hu Fen mocked.
Praised in the appraisal for supreme schemes, for bending Mao Jiong, and for surprising Dong Yuan.
Praised in the appraisal as a heroic talent recognized by Lu Kang who had admired Xue Xu’s expedition.
Cited in the appraisal as having been overcome by Tao Huang’s deep schemes.
Cited in the appraisal as having recognized Wu Yan’s talent.
Praised in the appraisal as the brilliant talent of southern Chu who held the northern march.
Cited in the encomium as surprised by Tao Huang’s stealth attack.
Cited in the encomium as the general whose expedition Wu Yan watched and admired.
